title: Maharani Jind Kaur
hook: his youngest queen, mother of Duleep Singh, would later defy an empire

segments.voice: Yesterday, painting at the court, with painters from Kangra among them, and your line, the court in paint. Today, a face from that court who will matter a great deal, and the week closes.

A woman's name keeps turning up in the letters of British officials, and not kindly. They write of her as difficult, even dangerous. They try to keep her away from her son, and move her from place to place. Years after the Maharaja is gone, she's still someone they worry about in the Punjab. Who was she? She began as the youngest of the Maharaja's queens.
screen: `A NAME IN OFFICIALS' LETTERS.` → `THEY CALL HER DANGEROUS.` → `THE YOUNGEST QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Sikh histories say Jind Kaur was the daughter of a man who looked after the royal kennels, not a princess from a great house. She married the Maharaja late in his life, the youngest of his queens, and gave birth to Duleep Singh, his youngest son. When the Maharaja died, the boy was still a baby, with older brothers and powerful ministers between him and the throne. Few would have guessed he'd ever sit on it. Without spoiling the story ahead: the throne of Lahore would pass through several hands, fast and violently, and in time it reached her son. Then Jind Kaur stood up as regent and spoke for him, in a court full of men, with a foreign empire at the border. She would be separated from him and imprisoned, and still she wouldn't give in. That's what it means to say she defied an empire, and you'll walk through it day by day. Look back at this week: Peshawar at the edge, the mountain of light, a court of many faiths, a ruler remembered for mercy, gifts to the Tenth Guru's places, the court in paint. A kingdom at its height, and standing quietly in it, a young queen whose courage hadn't yet been tested. The Gurus taught that a woman is not less: Guru Nanak asked why anyone would call her lowly, from whom kings are born. Jind Kaur would answer that question in her own way.
screen: `NOT A PRINCESS BY BIRTH.` · `MOTHER OF DULEEP SINGH.` · `A QUEEN WHO WOULD STAND UP.` · `A WEEK OF A KINGDOM AT ITS HEIGHT.` · then, large: `A BRAVE QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a mother who was brave: your own, a grandmother, a friend raising children alone, or one you've only read about. Picture her face and one hard thing she faced and didn't run from, and hold her in your mind with honor, breath by breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Jind Kaur, the youngest of the Maharaja's queens, mother of Duleep Singh, who would one day stand up to an empire for her son.
Your line: a brave queen. Her courage is still waiting for its test. Another week, walked.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharani Jind Kaur in histories of the end of the Sikh kingdom, and honor her as a mother and queen who would not give in.
